verse.text: Paul, a slave of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the faith of God’s chosen ones and the knowledge of the truth that accords with godliness,
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Many English versions soften it to 'servant' or 'bondservant'. In the Septuagint 'slave of God' is also a title of honour for figures such as Moses and the prophets, so the phrase carries both total belonging and dignity.

The preposition can mean 'in accordance with' or express aim ('with a view to'). The rendering takes it as the purpose of Paul's apostleship, which is to further the faith and knowledge of God's chosen people. This is the view of most recent interpreters. The alternative is that his apostleship conforms to the faith they hold.

verse.text: in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before long ages

note.traditional: before the world began; before time began; before times eternal

verse.note: The same adjective appears twice in this verse: 'eternal' life and, literally, 'age-long times'. It comes from the word for 'age', and in Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. With 'times' in the plural it looks back over the long ages of the past, so 'before time began' says slightly more than the Greek does. Many translations nonetheless take it as a reference to eternity past.

verse.text: and at the right time he revealed his word in the proclamation with which I was entrusted by the command of God our Savior,
to Titus, a true child in a shared faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
This is why I left you behind in Crete: so that you would set right what remained to be done and appoint elders in each town, as I directed you,
if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, with believing children who are not open to a charge of reckless living or insubordinate.
verse.note: Literally 'a man of one woman'. The phrase has been taken to exclude polygamy, to exclude remarriage after divorce or a wife's death, or more generally to require marital faithfulness. Many recent interpreters favour the last ('faithful to his wife'), but the question remains disputed and the traditional wording leaves it open.

The adjective can mean 'believing' (sharing the faith) or 'faithful, trustworthy' (dependable and obedient children). Translations and commentators are divided. The explanation that follows, about not being wild or insubordinate, fits either reading.

verse.text: For the overseer, as God’s household manager, must be above reproach: not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not a heavy drinker, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain,
verse.note: The word was an ordinary term for a supervisor or guardian, and the English 'bishop' descends from it. The passage moves from 'elders' in verse 5 to 'the overseer' here without a break, so most scholars conclude that the two terms describe the same local leaders at this stage. The single bishop over a region is a later development.

The word denotes the person, often a trusted slave, who ran a household's affairs and property on the owner's behalf. 'Steward' is accurate but now suggests other roles to most readers. The image is of the congregation as God's household, with the overseer answerable to its owner.

verse.text: but hospitable, a lover of what is good, sensible, just, devout, self-controlled,
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. The adjective here is the one rendered 'righteous' elsewhere in the New Testament. In a list of virtues like this, paired with 'devout', it denotes fair and right dealing with other people. This was a conventional pairing in Greek moral language.

verse.text: holding firmly to the faithful word as it has been taught, so that he may be able both to encourage with healthy teaching and to rebuke those who speak against it.
verse.note: The verb means to be in good health, and the letters to Timothy and Titus use it repeatedly as a medical image for teaching that makes people well. 'Sound doctrine' is the traditional rendering, but 'sound' no longer suggests health to most readers. 'Healthy' also keeps the link with verse 13, where the same verb is used of people being 'healthy in the faith'.

verse.text: For there are many insubordinate people, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision,

note.traditional: they of the circumcision; the circumcision party

verse.note: The phrase refers to people of Jewish background. Here they are most likely Jewish members of the Christian communities on Crete, since Titus is expected to correct them. Whether they formed an organised group pressing Jewish observances on others is not certain, though verse 14 points to Jewish traditions and rules as the substance of their teaching.

verse.text: who must be silenced. They are overturning whole households, teaching what they ought not for the sake of shameful gain.
One of them, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, vicious beasts, lazy gluttons.”
verse.note: The line is a verse of Greek poetry traditionally attributed to Epimenides, a Cretan sage of the sixth century BC who was reputed to be a seer. Cretans had a proverbial reputation for lying in the ancient world. 'Prophet' reflects how such figures were regarded among Greeks and does not rank him with the prophets of Israel.

verse.text: This testimony is true. For this reason rebuke them sharply, so that they may be healthy in the faith,
not paying attention to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth.
To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; instead, both their mind and their conscience are defiled.
They profess to know God, but by their works they deny him, being detestable and disobedient and unfit for any good work.
But as for you, speak what befits healthy teaching.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for being in good health, and the letters to Timothy and Titus use it against teaching pictured as diseased. 'Sound' is the traditional rendering and is not wrong, but the medical image has faded from it. The same word recurs in verse 2 ('healthy in faith') and verse 8 ('healthy speech'), and is rendered the same way each time.

verse.text: Older men are to be sober, dignified, self-controlled, healthy in faith, in love, in endurance.
verse.note: This word names one of the classic Greek virtues: a steady, well-governed mind that keeps impulses in check. Its word-family runs through the chapter (verses 2, 4, 5, 6 and 12), asked in turn of older men, young women, younger men and all believers. English versions usually vary the rendering; here it is kept as 'self-control' throughout so the repetition can be heard. The verb in verse 4, usually translated 'train' or 'encourage', is from the same family, hence 'school in self-control'.

verse.text: Older women likewise are to bear themselves as befits what is sacred: not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, but teachers of what is good,
verse.note: The word describes what is fitting for sacred persons, places or rites, and was used of priestly conduct and religious ceremony. The traditional 'reverent' is weaker and suggests an inner attitude, where the Greek speaks of outward bearing suited to holy service. The rendering also keeps the link with 'befits' in verse 1.

verse.text: so that they may school the young women in self-control, to love their husbands, to love their children,
to be self-controlled, pure, workers at home, good, subject to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be reviled.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have a rare word meaning 'working at home'. Many later manuscripts have a common word differing by one letter, meaning 'staying at home' or 'keeping house', which lies behind the older English rendering. The following word, 'good', can also be read with this one ('good household managers'). Most editors and translations treat it as a separate item, as here, sometimes rendering it 'kind'.

verse.text: Urge the younger men likewise to be self-controlled.
In every respect present yourself as a model of good works, showing in your teaching integrity, dignity,
and healthy speech that is beyond reproach, so that the opponent may be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us.
Slaves are to be subject to their own masters in everything, to be pleasing, not talking back,
not pilfering, but showing all good faithfulness, so that in everything they may adorn the teaching of God our Saviour.
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people,
verse.note: This verb and the noun 'appearing' in verse 13 belong together. In the period they were used for a god's visible intervention to help and for the public arrival of a ruler, and 'saviour' was likewise a title given to gods and kings. The passage frames Christ's first coming and his awaited return as two such appearances.

note.traditional: that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men

verse.note: 'To all people' can attach either to 'bringing salvation' or to 'has appeared'. Most modern translations take the first, as here: the grace is saving for everyone. Some older versions take the second: the grace that saves has appeared to everyone.

verse.text: training us so that, renouncing irreverence and worldly desires, we might live with self-control, justly, and reverently in the present age,
verse.note: The Greek sets a noun and an adverb from one word-family against each other: what is renounced and how one is then to live. The family denotes proper reverence toward the divine, shown in conduct, and its absence. The traditional 'ungodliness' and 'godly' keep the pairing but are vague in modern English; 'irreverence' and 'reverently' keep it and are closer to how the words were used.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. The adverb here describes conduct that is right, especially toward other people, and 'justly' is the natural English for that. The related noun is rendered 'righteousness' in this translation, as in most English versions.

verse.text: awaiting the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ,

note.term: our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ
note.traditional: the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ

verse.note: In the Greek a single article governs 'God' and 'Saviour', which most grammarians and most modern translations take to mean one person: Jesus Christ is called 'our great God and Saviour'. The older rendering distinguishes two, God and Christ, and a minority take 'Jesus Christ' as explaining 'the glory' of God. 'Appearing of the glory' can also be read as 'glorious appearing'.

verse.text: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his very own, zealous for good works.

note.term: a people of his very own

verse.note: This rare word comes from the Greek Old Testament, where it describes Israel as God's treasured possession at Sinai (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; 14:2). The verse as a whole echoes Scripture's language of God redeeming Israel from its lawless deeds and cleansing a people for himself (Psalm 130:8; Ezekiel 37:23). The older 'peculiar' meant 'belonging specially to one owner', a sense the word has lost.

verse.text: Speak these things; urge and rebuke with all authority. Let no one look down on you.
Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey, to be ready for every good work,
to slander no one, not to pick fights, to be considerate, showing all gentleness to all people.
verse.note: The traditional 'meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a considerate, unassertive way of treating others, and 'gentleness' or 'humility' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

verse.text: For we too were once senseless, disobedient, led astray, enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures, spending our lives in malice and envy, detestable, hating one another.
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for humanity appeared,
verse.note: The Greek word, philanthrōpia, was a stock term for the generosity expected of gods, kings and public benefactors toward those in their care. Together with 'appeared' and 'Savior', it is language a first-century reader would recognise from the public praise of rulers, here applied to God.

verse.text: it was not because of works we ourselves had done in righteousness but in keeping with his mercy that he saved us, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: 'righteousness' here and 'justified' in verse 7 share a root, as do 'righteous' and 'just'. The contrast is deliberate: it was not our own right conduct that saved us, but God's grace that set us right.

note.term: the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit
note.traditional: the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost

verse.note: The Greek can mean one washing that brings both rebirth and renewal, the Spirit being the agent of both, or two things: a washing of rebirth, and a renewal by the Spirit. The rendering leaves this open, as the Greek does. Most interpreters take the 'washing' to refer to baptism, though some understand it as a figure for inner cleansing.

verse.text: whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,
so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer 'life of the age to come'.

verse.text: The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may take care to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and useful to people.
verse.note: This translation normally renders the adjective 'faithful' or 'believing', but in current English a saying is not called faithful. The sense here is that the statement can be relied on, so 'trustworthy' is used. The formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and here most likely points back to the summary in verses 4 to 7.

note.traditional: be careful to maintain good works

verse.note: The verb can mean to take the lead in something, to busy oneself with it, or to practise a trade. Most translations take it as applying oneself to good deeds. A minority reading is 'engage in honourable occupations', which would also fit verse 14 with its mention of meeting needs.

verse.text: But keep clear of foolish debates, genealogies, quarrels, and fights over the law, for they are useless and empty.
After a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a divisive person,

note.traditional: a man that is an heretic

verse.note: The Greek word is the source of the English 'heretic', but in this period it described someone who forms a faction or causes division, not someone who holds a formally condemned doctrine. That later sense developed in the following centuries. Most modern translations likewise have 'divisive' or 'factious'.

verse.text: knowing that such a person is warped and goes on sinning, self-condemned.
When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there.
verse.note: Several cities bore this name, which means 'victory city'. The one meant is usually thought to be Nicopolis in Epirus, on the west coast of Greece, a port where a traveller could wait out the winter when sea voyages stopped.

verse.text: Make every effort to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, so that they lack nothing.
verse.note: The word means an expert in law. In the Gospels it refers to experts in the Jewish law, and the same adjective is used in verse 9 of disputes 'over the law'. Since Zenas has a Greek name, he may have been a jurist in Roman or Greek law, and the text does not settle which.

The verb means more than saying goodbye. It was the usual term for equipping travellers with food, money and whatever else they needed for the next stage of a journey, which is why the sentence continues 'so that they lack nothing'.

verse.text: And let our own people also learn to devote themselves to good works to meet pressing needs, so that they will not be unfruitful.
All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with all of you.
verse.note: The letter is addressed to Titus alone, but the closing 'you' is plural. The blessing reaches past him to the congregations in Crete, who were evidently expected to hear the letter read.
